title: Katha traditions
hookLine: different schools explain Gurbani in different styles

lines: THE MUSIC STOPS. A VOICE BEGINS.
cards: The kirtan ends. The instruments are set aside, and someone sits facing the sangat with the scripture open nearby. No singing now, just talking.
They take a single line sung a few minutes ago and open it: what each word means, which story it brings to mind, what it asks of a person on an ordinary Tuesday.
At another gurdwara next week, someone will open the same line in a completely different way. Both are doing katha, explanation. Today is about the different traditions of doing it.

teach.b: First, what katha is. The word means telling, or explanation. In a gurdwara, katha is the spoken part beside the sung part: a giani, a learned explainer, takes Gurbani and opens it for the sangat.

teach.h: WORD BY WORD, STORY, OR LINEAGE.
teach.b: Some explainers go word by word, giving the meaning of each term and how it fits the grammar of the line. Some tell sakhis, stories from the lives of the Gurus, and let the story carry the meaning.
Some draw on the vocabulary of older Indian philosophy, as the Nirmala and Udasi scholars did.
Some trace their reading through a teaching lineage; the Damdami Taksal, for one, says its line of teachers goes back to Guru Gobind Singh.
And some speakers today explain with history, science or everyday life, for listeners who grew up far from Punjab. Third, why there are many ways.
In the sixteenth pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: if anyone tries to tell of it and reflect on it, there is no counting what the Creator has made.
If the subject is that wide, no single explanation can finish it. Each school holds up a lamp to one part of a very large room. Fourth, how Sikhs hold the differences.
Explainers sometimes disagree, and Sikhs argue about which readings are faithful; that argument is part of a living tradition.

teach.h: THE LINE SITS ABOVE THEM ALL.
teach.b: Above all of them sits the Guru Granth Sahib itself.
The katha is a servant of the line, never its replacement.

how: In gurdwaras a giani may give katha after kirtan, explaining a line or hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib; explainers from different schools use word-by-word meaning, stories of the Gurus, or present-day examples.

the many styles of explaining Gurbani aloud
the order of hymns sung at a Sikh wedding

p: stories from the lives of the Gurus
no counting what the Creator made

s: there is one official way to explain Gurbani
explainers go word by word, tell stories, follow lineages, or use everyday life.
katha is the spoken explanation that sits beside kirtan
a giani takes a line of Gurbani and opens it for the sangat.
in Sikh practice the explanation outranks the scripture
the Guru Granth Sahib sits above every explainer; katha serves the line.

games.q: you hear the same line explained two different ways in two weeks. what do you do?
o: decide one explainer is wrong and stop listening.
hold both and ask what each lets you see.
stop listening to explanations at all.
games.why: Sikhs do argue about faithful readings, but the line sits above all the explainers. in paraphrase, Japji says there's no counting what the Creator has made.

practice: Bring to mind one line of scripture you know, from any book that matters to you, and two ways you've heard it explained or could read it. Hold the first and see what it lights up, then the second, without choosing.
Then let the line itself sit in the middle, bigger than both.

wordCard.voice: Katha traditions. The schools and styles of explaining Gurbani aloud: word by word, through stories, through teaching lineages, through everyday life. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: telling, explanation; the spoken exposition of Gurbani.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways to explain. Many lamps, and the room is bigger than all of them. Rest well.
